output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes lean clearly hawkish. On inflation, several participants cited still-elevated core services and core goods inflation, some judged underlying inflation above 2 percent and moving sideways, several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations, and many reported increased business cost pressures; almost all judged inflation risks tilted to the upside with upside risks from energy prices, the AI buildout, and possible further tariffs. On the labor market, a majority saw recent strengthening and participants generally viewed it near maximum employment with balanced risks, though several noted unusually low dynamism and some said aggregate wage growth was moderate and not inflationary. On policy, all supported the 1/4-point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many framed a higher path as prudent insurance, a number saw it necessary on their modal outlook, several viewed policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, and most expected another increase by year end. What would change minds: participants emphasized data dependence, with future decisions hinging on incoming information and the balance of risks. Net implication for the December 9 decision is hawkish (tilt +7), tempered only by dovish notes on low labor dynamics, moderate wages, and unsupportive housing conditions.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes are strongly hawkish. Participants judged inflation elevated with insufficient recent progress; several cited elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, some cited model-based underlying inflation above 2 percent, and several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations. Inflation risks were seen as skewed to the upside (some said more so), with many warning elevated energy prices and further tariffs could broaden pressures. The labor market was judged stable and near maximum employment, with a majority seeing recent strengthening, though some noted moderate wage growth and that the labor market was not a source of inflation pressure (the only clearly dovish notes). On policy, all supported the 25bp hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many favored a higher path on risk-management grounds, a number on their modal outlooks, several viewed policy as not or only mildly restrictive, and most expected another increase by year end. These are directly relevant to the December 9 decision and tilt hawkish, tempered only by explicit data-dependence language and a few dovish inflation/labor observations. Net tilt +7 bp.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes are strongly hawkish. All participants backed a 1/4-point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and 'most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end,' directly pointing toward further tightening at the December 9 decision. On inflation, participants saw it as still elevated with insufficient progress, several citing elevated core services and goods prices, elevated short-term inflation expectations, and inflation risks 'skewed to the upside,' with energy prices and possible further tariffs as upside risks. On the labor market, a majority saw recent strengthening and the market near maximum employment, though several noted unusually low dynamism and some judged wage growth moderate and not inflationary; labor risks were seen as broadly balanced. Many favored a higher path on risk-management grounds and several viewed current policy as 'not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.' The main dovish offsets are the methodology-related PCE adjustment, moderate wage commentary, and balanced labor risks. What would change minds: participants stressed decisions 'would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks.' Net lean is hawkish, warranting a positive tilt.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes are decisively hawkish. On inflation, participants judged it 'remained elevated and that they had not seen sufficient progress,' with several citing elevated core services ex-housing and core goods, some seeing underlying inflation above target, and several noting elevated short-term inflation expectations. On the labor market, a majority saw it had 'strengthened a bit recently' and participants generally viewed it 'close to maximum employment,' though several noted low dynamism and some said wage growth was moderate and not inflationary. On risks, participants 'generally assessed inflation risk as skewed to the upside' while labor risks were 'broadly balanced.' On policy, all supported the 1/4-point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many framed a higher path as prudent risk management, several saw the rate as 'not restrictive or only mildly restrictive,' and 'most participants assessed that another increase... would likely be appropriate by year end.' What would change their minds: 'decisions at future meetings would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks.' With the next decision on 2026-12-09, the explicit majority expectation of a further year-end hike drives a net hawkish tilt of +6 bp, tempered modestly by data-dependence and some dovish labor observations.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes are clearly hawkish. On inflation, several participants saw elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, some judged underlying inflation above 2% and moving sideways, several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations, and many cited business reports of rising cost pressures; only a few noted a declining 3-month core measure (with caveats). On the labor market, a majority saw recent strengthening and participants generally viewed it near maximum employment, though several noted unusually low dynamism and some said wages were not an inflation source. On risks, participants generally saw inflation risk skewed to the upside (some more so recently), with many worried about energy spillovers, some about AI-driven demand, and several about tariffs. On policy, all supported the 25bp hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many framed a higher path as prudent insurance, a number saw it as necessary on their modal outlook, several viewed the rate as not restrictive, and most expected another increase by year end. They stressed data dependence and an open mind as the condition for changing course. Net lean for the December 9, 2026 decision is hawkish (+7).
